items.question: 1/4 in vs 1/2 in router bit shank: which should a beginner buy?
items.short_answer: Start with 1/4 in (6.35 mm) shank. It fits any small or mid-size router. Move to 1/2 in only when your router is 2 HP or more and you cut deep profiles in hardwood.

items.question: How many router bits do you actually need? 6, 12 or 15 pieces?
items.short_answer: A 12-piece set is the practical sweet spot for most furniture and shelving work. Six is too few; fifteen mostly adds 1/2 in shank duplicates. Count profiles, not pieces.

items.question: What specs actually matter when buying a router bit set?
items.short_answer: Check four things: exact shank diameter (1/4 or 1/2 in), micro-grain carbide, sealed replaceable bearings, and how many distinct profiles the set contains. HRC numbers are marketing for wood cutting.

items.question: Carbide or high-speed steel: which router bits are worth the money?
items.short_answer: Buy carbide for anything used more than ten times; it lasts 10-25x longer than HSS in hardwood. HSS is only worth it for one-off softwood jobs.

items.question: 45, 55, 60, 65 degree router bits: what does the angle actually change?
items.short_answer: The angle describes cutting geometry: lower angles clear chips faster with more tear-out, higher angles give a cleaner finish in harder material at a slower feed. Ask sellers what the number refers to before comparing listings.

items.question: Cobalt or regular HSS drill bits for stainless steel?
items.short_answer: Use M35 cobalt (5% Co) with a 135 degree split point for stainless steel, at 300-500 rpm with constant pressure and cutting fluid. Regular HSS work-hardens stainless and dulls within a few holes.

items.question: Why does my diamond blade chip porcelain tile, and how do I stop it?
items.short_answer: Porcelain chips when you use a segmented blade at high rpm. Use a continuous-rim diamond blade at the low end of its rpm rating, wet if possible, and check the flange and 22.23 mm bore for wobble.

items.question: What grit sequence should I use when sanding wood?
items.short_answer: Double the grit roughly each step: 60, 120, 240, then 400 between finish coats. Each grit removes the previous grit's scratches; skipping steps wastes paper and leaves visible scratches.

items.question: Why is a $59 router bit set better than a $39 one?
items.short_answer: The difference is usually carbide grade, replaceable sealed bearings, shank tolerance and whether the advertised 12 profiles are actually 12 distinct shapes. A $39 set is rational for one softwood job; for MDF or oak used monthly, a dull bit burns the workpiece and the saving disappears.

items.question: 2, 3 or 4 flute end mill: which one for which material?
items.short_answer: 3-flute for aluminium, 4-flute for steel, 2-flute for plastics and deep slots. A 4-flute in aluminium clogs and welds; a 3-flute with polished or DLC flutes is the standard choice for non-ferrous work.

items.question: HRC55 or HRC65 end mills: is the harder grade worth it?
items.short_answer: HRC65 only pays off on hardened steel above about 45 HRC. On mild steel, stainless and aluminium, HRC55 is tougher, cheaper and finishes more parts before failing.

items.question: What is the actual difference between an aluminium end mill and a steel end mill?
items.short_answer: Aluminium end mills use 2-3 flutes, polished or DLC surfaces and a higher rake for chip clearance; steel end mills use 4 flutes, AlTiN coating and a stronger edge. Using one in the other material causes welding or rapid wear.

items.question: 3.175 mm, 6 mm or 8 mm shank: how do I pick?
items.short_answer: Match the collet: 3.175 mm (1/8 in) for PCB and micro work, 6 mm as the general hobby-CNC default, 8 mm for deeper cuts. 6 mm and 1/4 in are not interchangeable — they differ by 0.35 mm.

items.question: M35 or M42 cobalt drill bits: which for stainless steel?
items.short_answer: M35 (5% cobalt) covers most stainless work and is more forgiving; M42 (8%) only pays off in production on hard stainless with controlled speed. Cutting speed of 300-500 rpm matters more than the grade.

items.question: Masonry bit, hammer bit or regular drill bit: what is the difference?
items.short_answer: Masonry bits have a carbide tip for brick and block; SDS hammer bits have a reinforced shank for rotary hammers on concrete; HSS twist bits are for metal and wood only. Using a masonry bit on steel destroys the tip instantly.

items.question: Continuous, segmented or turbo rim diamond blade: which one?
items.short_answer: Continuous rim for chip-free porcelain and glazed tile, segmented for fast rough cuts in concrete and block, turbo as the compromise on hard stone. Glazed visible tile always gets continuous rim.

items.question: 24T, 40T or 60T saw blade: which tooth count for which job?
items.short_answer: 24T for fast ripping in softwood, 40T as the general crosscut blade, 60T+ for fine trim and veneered ply. A high tooth count in thick hardwood overheats because the gullets cannot clear chips.

items.question: Bi-metal or TCT hole saw: which one lasts?
items.short_answer: Bi-metal hole saws cut wood, plastics and thin sheet metal; TCT saws cut brick, block and fibre cement. Running a bi-metal saw in masonry with hammer action destroys it in one hole.

items.question: What rpm should I run a router bit at?
items.short_answer: Reduce rpm as bit diameter increases: up to 25 mm can run 18,000-24,000 rpm, 25-50 mm around 14,000-18,000, 50-75 mm about 10,000-14,000, and anything larger 8,000-12,000 or slower. Check the maximum rpm stamped on the shank.
